slides.title: Revision — Storage vs Functions
slides.definition: In the previous lectures we learned how Solidity stores data — variables, arrays, structs, and mappings. But storing data alone is useless. A smart contract needs LOGIC. Logic comes through functions. Storage is the memory. Functions are the actions.
keyPoints: Variable — stores a single value: uint public age = 20
Array — stores multiple values of the same type: uint[] public marks
Struct — groups different types under one name: struct Student { string name; uint age; }
Mapping — links a key to a value: mapping(address => uint) public balances
Functions — define WHAT the contract does: read data, write data, receive ETH, validate conditions
Without functions, storage sits idle — functions are what make a smart contract BEHAVE like an application

slides.title: Smart Contract = Storage + Functions
slides.subtitle: The Two Pillars of Every Contract
slides.outcomeDesc: Every function call that modifies storage creates a TRANSACTION recorded permanently on-chain

slides.title: Part 1 — Function Anatomy: Every Word Explained
slides.subtitle: Break down each keyword — students must understand every piece before writing functions

codeBlocks.label: Complete Function — Labelled

keyPoints: function — keyword that tells Solidity 'we are defining an action'
add — the function NAME; like a button label; called by users and other contracts
(uint a, uint b) — PARAMETERS: input data the caller must provide; uint a = first number, uint b = second number
public — VISIBILITY: who can call this; public = anyone (wallet, contract, or internally)
pure — MUTABILITY: this function neither reads nor writes blockchain storage; just pure math
returns(uint) — OUTPUT type: this function sends back one unsigned integer to the caller
return a + b — the actual computation; Solidity evaluates this and sends the result back
practicalSteps: Deploy Calculator contract in Remix
Call add(10, 20) → result: 30
Call add(100, 255) → result: 355
Notice: no transaction hash — pure functions are FREE (no gas when called externally)

slides.title: Part 2 — view vs pure: Reading the Blockchain
leftItems: Can READ state variables but CANNOT modify them
Has access to: state variables, block.timestamp, msg.sender, block.number
FREE when called externally by a wallet or dApp (zero gas cost)
Costs gas only when called internally from a state-changing transaction
Example: function getAge() public view returns(uint) { return age; }
Use when: you need to return a stored value like a balance, name, or count
Compiler enforces: if view accidentally writes state → compile error
slides.rightTitle: pure — No Blockchain Access At All
rightItems: CANNOT read OR write any state variable — completely isolated
No access to: msg.sender, block.timestamp, storage variables — nothing from chain
Only works with its own input parameters and local variables
FREE when called externally — purely off-chain computation
Example: function multiply(uint a, uint b) public pure returns(uint) { return a * b; }
Use when: utility math functions, string manipulation, calculations with no chain data
Compiler enforces: if pure reads state → compile error — use as documentation + safety

slides.title: Part 3 — State Changing Functions
slides.subtitle: Functions that WRITE to blockchain storage — these create real transactions and cost gas

codeBlocks.label: Counter Contract — State Change Demo

keyPoints: count++ — increments the state variable; this WRITES to blockchain storage slot 0
NO view or pure keyword — absence of these means the function modifies state
Every call to increment() creates a TRANSACTION: signed by wallet, broadcast to network, included in a block
Gas cost: each SSTORE (storage write) costs 20,000 gas for new slot or 5,000 gas to update existing
In Remix you will see: a green transaction hash and gas used in the console — this is proof of on-chain state change
Before increment(): count = 0 | After one call: count = 1 | After five calls: count = 5
getCount() is view — free when called by wallet; ONLY increment/decrement/reset cost gas
practicalSteps: Deploy Counter — count starts at 0
Call increment() → watch transaction appear in Remix console
Call count() → 1
Call increment() 4 more times → count = 5
Call reset() → count = 0
Observe: increment has a transaction hash, count (view) does not

slides.title: Part 4 — msg.sender: Who Is Calling?
slides.subtitle: The most important global variable in Solidity — the identity of the caller

codeBlocks.label: User Identity Contract

keyPoints: msg.sender — a global Solidity variable; always equals the address of whoever called the current function
Type: address — it is a 20-byte Ethereum address like 0x742d...f44e
In constructor: msg.sender = the wallet that DEPLOYED the contract — use this to set the owner
In a regular function: msg.sender = whoever sent the transaction calling that function
If Contract A calls Contract B: msg.sender inside B = address of Contract A — not the original human wallet
tx.origin = the ORIGINAL human wallet (always) — but using tx.origin for auth is a security risk
msg.sender is the foundation of ALL access control in Solidity: onlyOwner, roles, allowlists
practicalSteps: Deploy — owner is automatically set to your MetaMask wallet
Call whoAmI() → returns your wallet address
Call isOwner() → true (you are the deployer)
Switch to a different account in Remix → call isOwner() → false
Call saveUser() from different account → lastCaller updates to that account

slides.title: msg.sender — The Caller Identity Flow
slides.subtitle: Part 4 — msg.sender
slides.explanation: Every time a function is called, msg.sender is automatically set by the EVM to the address that sent the transaction. It cannot be faked — the wallet's private key signs the transaction, and the EVM verifies the signature.
slides.realWorld: Who is msg.sender in each scenario:
slides.syntaxNote: Set in constructor to capture the deployer. Used with require() to restrict who can call sensitive functions.

slides.title: Part 5 — payable Functions: Receiving ETH
slides.subtitle: Without the payable keyword, a function CANNOT receive ETH — the transaction will REVERT

codeBlocks.label: Wallet Contract — Deposit & Balance

keyPoints: payable — keyword that allows a function to accept ETH; without it, sending ETH to that function causes an automatic revert
address(this).balance — returns the total ETH balance held by THIS contract in wei (1 ETH = 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 wei)
Wei is the smallest ETH unit: 1 ETH = 10^18 wei; getBalance() returns a very large uint256 number
ETH sent to deposit() is credited to the contract's balance automatically by the EVM
receive() external payable — special function called when ETH is sent to the contract with NO function call data
fallback() external payable — called when ETH arrives with data that matches no known function signature
In Remix: change value to '1 ether' in the Value field, then call deposit() — check getBalance() shows 1000000000000000000
practicalSteps: Deploy Wallet contract
In Remix: set Value field to '1 ether'
Call deposit() — observe transaction succeeds
Call getBalance() → 1000000000000000000 (1 ETH in wei)
Send 0.5 ETH → call getBalance() → 1500000000000000000
Try calling deposit() with 0 ETH → getBalance() unchanged → still works (0 ETH deposited)

slides.title: Part 6 — msg.value: How Much ETH Was Sent?
slides.subtitle: msg.value gives you the exact amount of ETH the caller included in the transaction

codeBlocks.label: msg.value Demo Contract

keyPoints: msg.value — uint256; the amount of ETH (in wei) included in the current transaction; only accessible in payable functions
msg.value = 0 for non-payable calls; attempting to access msg.value in a non-payable function = compile error
0.01 ether — Solidity understands ether as a unit suffix; 0.01 ether = 10000000000000000 wei (10^16)
Other unit suffixes: 1 wei, 1 gwei (10^9 wei), 1 ether (10^18 wei) — all compile-time constants
deposits[msg.sender] += msg.value — accumulates each caller's total ETH deposits in a mapping
require(msg.value >= 0.01 ether) — minimum payment enforcement; same pattern used in NFT minting contracts
Real DeFi use: Uniswap, Aave, Compound all use msg.value to receive ETH in their deposit/swap functions
practicalSteps: Deploy ValueDemo
Set Value to '1 ether' → call deposit() → returns 1000000000000000000
Set Value to '0.001 ether' → call depositMinimum() → REVERTS: 'Minimum deposit is 0.01 ETH'
Set Value to '0.05 ether' → call depositMinimum() → succeeds

slides.title: Part 7 — require(): Protecting the Contract
slides.subtitle: Smart contracts must validate all conditions before executing — require() is the primary guard

codeBlocks.label: require() + revert() Demo

keyPoints: require(condition, 'error message') — if condition is FALSE: transaction REVERTS; error message is returned; all state changes undone
require(condition, 'error message') — if condition is TRUE: execution continues normally to next line
Gas behaviour: all gas consumed UP TO the require() that failed is kept by validator; gas NOT yet used is refunded
Multiple require() in one function — each checked in order from top to bottom; first false one stops execution
revert('reason') — manually triggers a revert; identical behaviour to require(false, 'reason'); used in complex if-else logic
assert(condition) — for internal invariants that should NEVER be false; uses Panic error type; does NOT refund gas (use sparingly)
require() is used for: access control (only owner), input validation (amount > 0), state checks (not paused, sufficient balance)
practicalSteps: Deploy with Wallet A (owner) → call ownerAction() → 'Welcome, Owner!'
Switch to Wallet B → call ownerAction() → REVERTS: 'Not the owner'
Call deposit(0) → REVERTS: 'Amount must be greater than 0'
Call deposit(100) → succeeds → vaultBalance = 100
Call withdraw(200) as owner → REVERTS: 'Insufficient balance'
Call withdraw(50) as owner → succeeds → vaultBalance = 50

flows.label: When condition is TRUE
flows.note: Normal path — everything proceeds. Transaction succeeds. Gas used. Block recorded.

flows.label: When condition is FALSE
flows.note: Protection path — error message returned. Gas up to revert is consumed. No state change persists.

slides.title: Final Practical — Simple Bank Contract
slides.subtitle: Combines everything from this lecture: payable, msg.sender, msg.value, require() — a real DeFi foundation

codeBlocks.label: SimpleBank.sol — Full Contract

keyPoints: address public owner — set in constructor to msg.sender (deployer); used for access control
mapping(address => uint) public balances — each wallet tracks its own deposit total separately
deposit() payable — receives ETH; require(msg.value > 0) rejects zero-value calls; adds msg.value to caller's balance
address(this).balance — total ETH held by the contract across ALL depositors combined
balances[msg.sender] — each caller sees ONLY their own balance; complete isolation between users
ownerPanel() — require(msg.sender == owner) gatekeeps; anyone else calling gets revert 'Not Owner'
This is the foundation of: DeFi staking vaults, escrow contracts, multi-sig wallets, yield farming protocols
practicalSteps: Deploy — owner = your wallet
Wallet A: set value to '1 ether' → call deposit() → myBalance() = 1 ETH in wei
Wallet B: set value to '0.5 ether' → call deposit() → myBalance() = 0.5 ETH in wei
Call getContractBalance() → 1.5 ETH in wei (combined)
Wallet A: call myBalance() → only sees their 1 ETH (not Wallet B's)
Owner calls ownerPanel() → 'Welcome, Bank Owner!'
Non-owner calls ownerPanel() → REVERTS: 'Not Owner'

slides.title: Real-World Connections — What You Can Build Now
leftItems: State changing functions → any counter, vote tally, score tracker, inventory system
msg.sender + mapping → per-user data storage; every DeFi protocol uses mapping(address=>uint) for user balances
payable + msg.value → token sale (ICO), NFT mint price enforcement, crowdfunding contract, donation contract
require(msg.sender == owner) → admin panels, fee withdrawal, emergency pause — the onlyOwner pattern
require(msg.value >= price) → NFT mint: require(msg.value >= 0.08 ether, 'Wrong price') — exact same code used by real NFT projects
address(this).balance → treasury balance display in DAOs and staking contracts
rightItems: Task 1: Voting Contract — add candidate names (array), vote() function increments count for a candidate, require that each address can only vote once using mapping(address => bool)
Task 2: Piggy Bank — deposit ETH, only owner can withdraw all ETH using transfer(), add require that balance > 0 before withdrawing
Task 3: Auction Contract — store highestBid (uint) and highestBidder (address), bid() function is payable; require new bid > highestBid; update both variables
Challenge: Add a minimum deposit amount to SimpleBank — require(msg.value >= 0.01 ether) and add an event Deposited(address indexed user, uint amount) that emits on every successful deposit
Explore: Read the Uniswap V2 Router source code on Etherscan — find msg.sender, msg.value, and require() usage in their swap functions

slides.title: Lecture #4 Summary — Key Takeaways
points: A function has five parts: keyword, name, parameters, visibility+mutability, return type — understand every word before writing
view reads state (free externally); pure does zero chain access (free externally); no modifier = state-changing (costs gas, creates a transaction)
State-changing functions write to storage with SSTORE — each call creates a signed transaction, broadcast to network, included in a block permanently
msg.sender is the 20-byte address of whoever called the function — the cornerstone of ALL access control in Solidity; set owner = msg.sender in constructor
payable functions can receive ETH; address(this).balance holds the contract's total ETH; msg.value holds exactly how much ETH this specific call included
require(condition, 'message') is your primary guard — false condition → REVERT; all state changes undone; error message returned to caller; gas up to revert is kept
SimpleBank combines all concepts: payable deposit, per-user mapping balances, owner access control with require, address(this).balance for total — the DeFi pattern
slides.closing: Functions are the actions that bring storage to life. Master these seven concepts and you can read and write ANY real Solidity contract.
